title: Kickoff: Latency per Dollar benchmark report (xfn)
summary: Cross-functional kickoff for the public “latency per dollar” benchmark report. Team aligned on goals (credible methodology + GTM), initial scope (chat + embeddings baselines, NA/EU + one APAC region), constraints (no production SLO impact, no over-claiming, no raw logs), and a 6–8 week timeline. Perf/Evals to own workload definition + rerun/variance policy; SRE to own capacity windows + guardrails; Docs/Marketing to own landing page/PDF narrative + claim language and approvals. Next steps include locking model/region matrix, confirming caching/batching policy for consistency, and drafting methodology FAQ and claim disclaimers.
topics:
1) Success criteria and audience (engineers + procurement)
2) Benchmark scope: workloads, models, regions, and what’s public
3) Methodology details: warmups, caching, batching, concurrency, and units for latency/$
4) Risk management: variance, cherry-picking perception, SLO impact, and messaging approvals
5) Launch plan dependencies: landing page, PDF, charts, UTM/attribution
6) Ownership and timeline
next_steps: Perf/Evals to circulate proposed workload definitions (chat + embeddings) with exact distributions and measurement windows by EOW
SRE to propose capacity windows per region and production guardrails/rollback criteria
Marketing to draft landing page wirecopy + narrative outline for internal review (include disclaimers and what the metric does/doesn’t mean)
Docs to propose placement for methodology appendix + “how to reproduce” guidance and cross-links
Tyler (MOPs) to propose UTM plan + conversion events (download, signup, book-a-consult) and confirm attribution setup
Camila/Jonas to confirm approval checklist for external claims and reviewers needed for sign-off
action_items: Claire Dubois: Draft benchmark workload spec (prompts, input distributions, sequence lengths, concurrency targets) and share for review by 2025-01-31
Rina Kobayashi: Validate benchmark harness supports cross-region runs with consistent config; list any missing flags by 2025-02-03
Sana Farid: Propose variance analysis approach (rerun thresholds, confidence band language) by 2025-02-04
Sean Gallagher: Draft SRE run plan (monitoring dashboards, alerts, stop conditions) by 2025-02-05
Vanessa Ortiz: Tentatively hold capacity windows for NA/EU/APAC regions; share candidate dates by 2025-02-05
Elliot Price: Create doc skeleton for methodology appendix + FAQ section by 2025-02-06
Wei Chen: Draft “how to reproduce” outline (customer-safe, minimal) by 2025-02-06
Ethan Wallace: Assemble report outline + list of required charts (inputs needed from Perf/Evals) by 2025-02-07
Tyler Benson: Confirm UTM taxonomy + tracking plan and share with web/docs by 2025-02-07
Ben Carter: Consolidate scope decisions (models/regions/workloads) into a single source of truth doc and schedule review meeting by 2025-02-07
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Kickoff: Latency per Dollar benchmark report (xfn)
Date: 2025-01-28
Time: 17:02 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees (Redwood): Ben Carter (Growth/Campaign), Camila Reyes (Marketing), Ethan Wallace (Report narrative), Jonas Weber (Applied ML sponsor), Claire Dubois (Perf/Evals), Rina Kobayashi (Perf/Evals), Sana Farid (Stats/variance), Sean Gallagher (SRE), Neha Kapoor (Capacity/SLO guardrails), Vanessa Ortiz (Capacity windows), Elliot Price (Docs/web), Wei Chen (Docs), Tyler Benson (Marketing Ops)

----

[00:00] Ben Carter: Alright, we’re at time. Thanks everyone. This is the kickoff for the latency per dollar benchmark report. The end goal is a public report, landing page, downloadable PDF, charts, the whole launch kit. I’ll do quick intros and then we can lock scope and risks.

[00:18] Camila Reyes: Hey, Camila. Exec sponsor on marketing side. Goal for me is, uh, credibility. We do not want a “we’re fastest” blog post that gets shredded on Hacker News. We want a methodology people can actually reproduce.

[00:33] Jonas Weber: Jonas, Applied ML. I’ll be the methodology sign-off. We should treat this like a paper-ish artifact: define the workload, define the test conditions, and be super explicit about limitations.

[00:45] Claire Dubois: Claire, Perf and evals. I’ll run the execution with Rina. We’ve already got the harness mostly there, but we need to agree on what is “production-like” without… inventing a whole universe.

[00:57] Rina Kobayashi: Rina. I’m the one who will push the button and regret it later. (laughs) Mostly I’ll own the runner and the config consistency across regions.

[01:06] Sana Farid: Sana. I’ll focus on variance and confidence intervals… or at least, language that doesn’t overstate precision.

[01:14] Sean Gallagher: Sean, SRE. We’ll keep this from, uh, melting production. Capacity windows, guardrails, monitoring. We need to do it cleanly.

[01:23] Neha Kapoor: Neha, guardrails sponsor. Please do not run a benchmark suite on the same cluster that’s serving real traffic unless we have hard limits and a kill switch.

[01:33] Vanessa Ortiz: Vanessa, capacity. I’ll coordinate holds on GPU pools by region.

[01:39] Elliot Price: Elliot, docs and web publishing. We’ll need the landing page, appendix, and cross links.

[01:46] Wei Chen: Wei, docs. I can take first pass at the methodology FAQ and the “how to reproduce” section.

[01:53] Tyler Benson: Tyler, marketing ops. I’ll handle UTMs, attribution, events for download -> signup -> book a consult.

[02:02] Ben Carter: Cool. Agenda: success criteria, scope (models/regions/workloads), methodology decisions that block us, then launch timeline and owners.

[02:13] Ben Carter: Success criteria: 1) establish Redwood as the reference for production economics, “latency per dollar,” 2) drive inbound for Hosted API and also Dedicated/Private conversations, 3) arm sales with talk tracks. Anything to add?

[02:30] Camila Reyes: Add: defensibility. The report should survive competitor scrutiny. People will ask “what about caching,” “what about pricing,” “what about region.” We should pre-answer.

[02:43] Jonas Weber: And reproducibility. We can’t publish raw logs, but we can publish enough that a customer can run a smaller variant and see the same pattern.

[02:55] Ben Carter: Great. Let’s do scope. Claire, you want to propose workloads?

[03:00] Claire Dubois: Sure. We think two baselines. One chat workload: mixed prompt lengths, some short, some moderate, target output tokens. And one embeddings baseline: fixed input distribution, batch size constraints. For chat, we should include concurrency, because without concurrency it’s basically a microbenchmark.

[03:20] Rina Kobayashi: The harness already supports concurrency sweeps, but we need to pick like… one or two representative settings, otherwise charts explode.

[03:29] Sana Farid: If we pick one, it will be criticized as cherry-picked. If we pick too many, it’s unreadable. Maybe we do a “standard profile” and then show sensitivity as a small appendix chart.

[03:43] Ethan Wallace: From narrative perspective, standard profile plus sensitivity appendix is a good compromise. Main story stays clean.

[03:52] Ben Carter: What’s the “standard profile” mean in numbers?

[03:56] Claire Dubois: Tentatively: chat at, say, concurrency 16 and 64? With a distribution of input tokens, like median maybe 300-ish, and output like 150-ish. But we need to align with real production telemetry—Logan and Caleb aren’t here, but we can pull anonymized distributions.

[04:18] Sean Gallagher: From SRE: concurrency 64 across multiple models and regions might be… heavy. We can do it in a reserved window but we need a cap on QPS and GPU saturation.

[04:30] Neha Kapoor: Yeah. “Standard profile” also needs to be safe to run repeatedly. Remember we need reruns to handle variance.

[04:40] Camila Reyes: Are we including tool calling / structured outputs? Because marketing will want to say it’s representative.

[04:47] Jonas Weber: I’d avoid mixing features. We can mention we support those features but the benchmark is plain generation and embeddings. Otherwise the surface area is endless.

[04:58] Ethan Wallace: Agree. Keep it explainable.

[05:03] Ben Carter: Okay. Models and regions. We said curated set of popular open models. Jonas, any constraints?

[05:10] Jonas Weber: Must be models we can serve consistently across regions with the same runtime. Also we should avoid flipping quantization mid-report unless we call it out. The “apples to apples” narrative is critical.

[05:24] Claire Dubois: We can group by model family and size. Like “7B class,” “13B class,” “70B class.” But, it gets messy because families differ.

[05:34] Sana Farid: Grouping is fine as long as we don’t imply family A beats family B universally. We should show results per model and provide the grouping as a lens.

[05:45] Ben Carter: Regions: we need NA and EU, and at least one APAC region. Mina isn’t here, but we should confirm which APAC region is stable for Hosted.

[05:55] Sean Gallagher: APAC region availability: we can do it, but capacity is tighter. If we pick APAC, please don’t pick the week where we’re doing fleet upgrades.

[06:05] Vanessa Ortiz: I can check. My guess is we can reserve windows in early Feb for NA/EU and mid-Feb for APAC. But I need exact model list to estimate hours.

[06:17] Elliot Price: From docs: region naming must match what users see. Also, we should clarify that results are per region and not “global.” People will screenshot one region chart and misinterpret.

[06:31] Wei Chen: Also for EU: data residency. We should be careful in wording: benchmark traffic is synthetic, no customer data. But EU prospects will ask whether the inference stays in EU region if they choose it.

[06:46] Camila Reyes: Yes, and we should avoid implying that picking EU gives you identical performance to NA. It won’t.

[06:55] Ben Carter: Good. Now, the metric: latency per dollar. There’s a lot of ways to compute it. Claire, what’s our definition?

[07:03] Claire Dubois: The simplest: tokens per second per dollar, or dollars per token times latency… But the chosen definition in the harness PR is basically “p50 latency divided by cost per request,” and then invert? Actually… Rina can you clarify what we implemented.

[07:18] Rina Kobayashi: Yeah. In the benchmark-lab output we’re computing cost per 1M tokens based on metered price for that model/region, then we compute latency per dollar as… okay, the code calls it “latency_per_dollar = p50_latency_ms / (cost_per_request_usd)” where cost per request is derived from token count * price per token. But we can also present “ms per $1” or the inverse “$ per ms” which is weird.

[07:46] Sana Farid: “Latency per dollar” as a phrase is ambiguous. People might think lower is better if it’s ms/$, but higher is better if it’s tokens/sec/$.

[07:56] Ben Carter: For marketing, we want an intuitive direction. Higher is better is easier for charts? Actually, not sure.

[08:04] Ethan Wallace: Depends. “Latency per $” sounds like “how much latency you buy for a dollar,” which should be lower is better. But we’ve been talking about “latency per dollar (better)” which is confusing.

[08:18] Camila Reyes: This is exactly why we need a glossary. We can pick a metric, but we need to label charts “lower is better” or “higher is better” consistently.

[08:28] Jonas Weber: We can define a primary metric and also include supporting metrics: throughput, p50, p95, cost per 1M tokens. Then people can sanity check.

[08:41] Sana Farid: I’d propose: pick one “production economics score” for headline, but publish the components. Otherwise it feels like we made up a magic number.

[08:53] Ben Carter: Let’s not call it a score. (laughs) But yes, components must be visible.

[09:00] Claire Dubois: For engineering sanity, I prefer we lead with “throughput per dollar” or “tokens per second per dollar.” But the project name is already latency per dollar.

[09:11] Camila Reyes: The reason we picked “latency per dollar” is it resonates with both engineers and procurement. Procurement asks “cost,” engineers ask “latency,” and this combines them. But we can define it as “p50 latency at a given throughput budget” maybe.

[09:27] Sean Gallagher: Please do not invent a “given throughput budget” unless it’s actually fixed in the experiment.

[09:33] Rina Kobayashi: What we can do: fix the workload profile (tokens in/out, concurrency) and then measure p50/p95 latency and compute $ per 1M tokens. Then show a derived ratio. That’s defensible.

[09:49] Sana Farid: Yes. And we should be explicit: “This ratio is only comparable under the same workload profile.” Big disclaimer.

[10:00] Ben Carter: Okay, provisional decision: we’ll keep the report name “latency per dollar” but in the methodology we define it precisely and we always show supporting metrics.

[10:11] Elliot Price: And in the FAQ: “Can I compare this to my workload?” answer: “Use the reproduce guide to test your distribution.”

[10:20] Wei Chen: We should also explain caching/batching settings because that changes unit economics drastically.

[10:28] Claire Dubois: Right. Let’s talk caching and batching. For comparability, we need fixed settings across runs. But production uses adaptive batching.

[10:40] Jonas Weber: We can set a policy: allow runtime’s standard batching, but disable “special” caching that would only benefit a repeated prompt set. Like, do warmup, but don’t let prefix cache from one run leak to another.

[10:57] Rina Kobayashi: The harness can clear caches between runs. But there’s also kernel autotuning warmup. We need consistent warmup duration per model.

[11:08] Sean Gallagher: Also, clearing caches between runs can spike GPU memory churn. We need to watch.

[11:15] Neha Kapoor: The bigger point: do not optimize specifically for the benchmark. If we tweak runtime flags for the suite, it should be explained and ideally match best practices for customers.

[11:28] Camila Reyes: Yes. Messaging risk: if we set weird flags and then customers don’t get that performance, we’ll get support tickets.

[11:38] Ethan Wallace: So we need to align: the config should reflect what a customer gets by default, or at least what’s recommended.

[11:45] Claire Dubois: I’ll coordinate with runtime team, but for now: default batching on, standard KV cache behavior, no persistent prefix cache across requests. Warmup: run for 2 minutes, measure for 10 minutes, repeated 3 times per model/region.

[12:06] Sana Farid: Three repeats is good, but we should decide thresholds for reruns. Like if p95 variance is more than X percent.

[12:15] Ben Carter: This is where the anomaly triage playbook comes in, right.

[12:18] Sana Farid: Exactly.

[12:21] Sean Gallagher: And we need reserved windows. We cannot run this during peak hours.

[12:26] Vanessa Ortiz: If we’re doing 3 repeats * multiple models * 3 regions, we’re talking… maybe dozens of GPU-hours. I’ll need the matrix.

[12:38] Ben Carter: Understood. We’ll lock the model/region matrix by end of week.

[12:44] Camila Reyes: On risks: besides SLO impact, we have “claims.” We need a do/don’t list. Like we can say “In our test, under these conditions, Redwood achieved X.” Not “Redwood is the fastest in the world.”

[12:59] Jonas Weber: Also we should avoid comparing to competitors unless we can validate. If we mention AWS or Google, it should be descriptive, not comparative, unless we run the exact same harness there. Which we probably won’t in this iteration.

[13:13] Ben Carter: The report should be “Redwood benchmark across models/regions on Redwood.” Not a vendor shootout.

[13:20] Ethan Wallace: We can still do competitive framing in the narrative: why production economics matters, pitfalls of simple token pricing, etc. But not “Vendor X is worse.”

[13:31] Camila Reyes: Great.

[13:33] Elliot Price: For docs/web, we need the approval checklist early because publishing is the last step and we don’t want a last-minute rewrite.

[13:42] Wei Chen: Yep. If we can get the disclaimers and definition language early, we can build it into the appendix.

[13:50] Tyler Benson: On tracking: we’ll have landing page views, PDF downloads, “copy table” clicks, and then conversion to signups or book demo. But the UTM plan needs to be consistent across social/email/partners.

[14:06] Ben Carter: Perfect. We’ll do a separate 20 minutes later this week on UTMs, but we’ll capture it as a dependency.

[14:15] Ben Carter: Let’s do timeline. We’re targeting a 6–8 week process. Is that realistic?

[14:21] Claire Dubois: If we don’t change scope midstream, yes. The biggest unknown is capacity windows and reruns.

[14:29] Sean Gallagher: We can make windows, but I need a “no surprises” rule: don’t add a new model the day before.

[14:37] Camila Reyes: Deal.

[14:39] Jonas Weber: Another risk: regional variability due to underlying hardware differences. If EU region uses different GPUs, we need to disclose.

[14:50] Rina Kobayashi: Some regions have different fleet mix. We can either constrain to one hardware class per region or disclose the actual hardware.

[15:01] Ben Carter: Are we allowed to disclose hardware?

[15:03] Sean Gallagher: We can disclose at a high level. “H100-class” vs exact SKU might be sensitive. But we can say “GPU type” if it’s already public in docs.

[15:13] Elliot Price: We have some region docs. We can align with whatever is public there.

[15:18] Camila Reyes: If we can’t disclose, we at least need to say “Results are for Redwood-hosted infrastructure in these regions; underlying hardware may vary by region.”

[15:29] Sana Farid: And in charts, we should not present tiny deltas as meaningful. If the difference is within noise, say so.

[15:38] Ethan Wallace: We can annotate with confidence bands or error bars—if we have the data.

[15:43] Sana Farid: We will.

[15:45] Ben Carter: Alright, I’m going to jump us to ownership. Perf/Evals owns: workload definition, harness execution, QA notes, final numbers. SRE owns: capacity windows, monitoring, stop conditions. Docs owns: appendix, reproduce guide, landing page technical accuracy. Marketing owns: narrative, charts layout, CTAs, channel plan. Agreement?

[16:12] (crosstalk)

[16:13] Sean Gallagher: Yes.

[16:13] Elliot Price: Yes.

[16:14] Claire Dubois: Yep.

[16:16] Camila Reyes: Yep.

[16:18] Ben Carter: Great. Let’s dig into methodology open questions we need to settle today so the team can start work.

[16:26] Ben Carter: One: Which metrics are public? Raw tables? Or only summarized charts?

[16:32] Camila Reyes: I want at least a public table. Engineers will ask for numbers.

[16:37] Jonas Weber: Public table is okay if sanitized: no internal IDs, no per-request logs, just aggregated metrics.

[16:44] Sean Gallagher: And no timestamps that let people infer capacity events.

[16:48] Wei Chen: Also careful about pricing fields. If pricing is public, fine. If not, we need to align with pricing page.

[16:55] Ben Carter: We’ll include “cost per 1M tokens” if that matches public pricing. Otherwise we show “relative cost index” which I don’t love.

[17:06] Camila Reyes: I’d rather align with pricing page and keep it real. If pricing is complicated, we can say “effective list price” and link.

[17:15] Tyler Benson: Linking to pricing page is good for conversion, honestly.

[17:18] Ethan Wallace: But careful: if pricing changes, the report ages fast.

[17:22] Jonas Weber: Then we version the report. “As of date.” That’s fine.

[17:29] Ben Carter: Two: caching/batching policy. We already said default batching on, no prompt prefix cache across runs, warmup then measure. Everyone okay?

[17:41] Claire Dubois: Yes, but we need to document exact runtime flags and versions.

[17:46] Rina Kobayashi: And pin model versions.

[17:49] Elliot Price: Great for docs: we can publish a config snippet in the reproduce guide.

[17:55] Ben Carter: Three: concurrency profile. Claire proposed 16 and 64; Sean flagged heaviness.

[18:02] Sean Gallagher: If you do both, do them sequentially and with hard caps. Maybe we treat 16 as “baseline” and 64 as “high concurrency” appendix.

[18:14] Camila Reyes: I like that. Main report: one profile. Appendix: sensitivity.

[18:21] Sana Farid: Works statistically too. We can keep the headline on one profile.

[18:27] Jonas Weber: Okay, standard profile: concurrency 16, plus token distribution. Appendix includes 64.

[18:35] Claire Dubois: I’m okay with that.

[18:38] Ben Carter: Great. Four: p50 vs p95. Which is primary?

[18:44] Camila Reyes: p95 matters for user experience, but it’s also noisier.

[18:49] Sean Gallagher: p95 will expose infra jitter. That’s real though.

[18:54] Sana Farid: We should report both. But for the derived metric, maybe use p50 to reduce noise, and show p95 separately.

[19:03] Jonas Weber: Agree.

[19:05] Ethan Wallace: We can phrase as: “p50 latency per dollar” with p95 as reliability of latency distribution.

[19:12] Camila Reyes: But careful: “reliability” is loaded. Let’s call it “tail latency.”

[19:18] Ethan Wallace: Good catch.

[19:22] Ben Carter: Five: region comparability. Are we using identical hardware across regions? If not, disclose. We’ll disclose.

[19:31] Vanessa Ortiz: In practice, some regions will have slightly different GPU types. I’ll see what we can constrain.

[19:38] Neha Kapoor: From guardrails: if we constrain to a smaller pool, we need to ensure it doesn’t impact customers.

[19:45] Sean Gallagher: Exactly.

[19:49] Ben Carter: Okay. Let’s talk about the “how to reproduce” guidance. Wei, what should it look like?

[19:56] Wei Chen: Minimal. Something like: “Here’s a script to run N requests with a similar token distribution, against a chosen region, capture p50/p95 and cost.” We should not include internal cluster details. Also, we need to mention people can use their own prompts.

[20:16] Elliot Price: We can host it as a docs page and link to a GitHub example.

[20:20] Ben Carter: Great.

[20:22] Camila Reyes: Another messaging point: we should be explicit this is about serving economics, not model quality. People will conflate.

[20:31] Jonas Weber: Yes. Add a section: “Quality held constant by using same model; this benchmark is about serving configuration and infra.” But even then, quantization can affect quality. If we use quantization, we must disclose.

[20:47] Claire Dubois: We do use quantized variants for some models for efficiency. If we do, we need to specify bits, and maybe provide a note that outputs may differ.

[20:57] Camila Reyes: Do we want that complication in v1?

[21:00] Claire Dubois: It’s reality. If we hide it, it’s misleading. But we can say “Redwood recommended serving profile” and then list it.

[21:11] Sana Farid: Disclose, and don’t compare across different quantization levels as if it’s identical. Or at least annotate.

[21:19] Ethan Wallace: For narrative, we can keep the main comparisons within the same model configuration. Like model X (profile A) in region Y.

[21:28] Ben Carter: Okay, we’ll have a “serving profile” column in the internal tables and decide what is public.

[21:36] Sean Gallagher: Please keep public content simple. Internally you can track everything; externally don’t overwhelm.

[21:43] Ben Carter: Understood.

[21:46] Ben Carter: Let’s capture risks and mitigation.

[21:50] Camila Reyes: Risk: perceived cherry-picking. Mitigation: publish inclusion criteria, show the full matrix, disclose limitations, include variance.

[22:02] Jonas Weber: Risk: methodology ambiguous. Mitigation: explicit definitions, pinned versions, publish reproduce guide.

[22:11] Sean Gallagher: Risk: production SLO impact. Mitigation: reserved windows, rate limits, monitoring, automatic stop.

[22:20] Neha Kapoor: Risk: benchmark config differs from customer defaults. Mitigation: align with recommended defaults; document flags; avoid weird one-off toggles.

[22:32] Elliot Price: Risk: doc/landing page says one thing, charts say another. Mitigation: single glossary and copy review pass by Perf/Evals.

[22:42] Tyler Benson: Risk: we can’t measure impact. Mitigation: tracking plan, UTMs, and consistent CTAs.

[22:49] Ben Carter: Great.

[22:52] Ben Carter: Quick question: do we mention competitors at all? People will ask.

[22:57] Camila Reyes: We can mention the broader landscape—AWS/GCP/Azure have managed endpoints, and there are LLM API providers like Together or Replicate. But we shouldn’t claim we beat them unless we test them.

[23:13] Jonas Weber: Agree.

[23:15] Ethan Wallace: We can focus on “why inference economics is hard” rather than “we’re best.”

[23:21] Ben Carter: Perfect.

[23:24] (silence)

[23:26] Ben Carter: Okay, last chunk: decisions recap, then next steps.

[23:31] Ben Carter: Decisions today:
- Workloads: chat + embeddings baseline.
- Standard profile: one main concurrency setting (16) with sensitivity appendix (64).
- Metrics: p50 and p95 reported; derived “latency/$” defined explicitly and always shown with components.
- Public data: aggregated table likely yes; no raw logs.
- Methodology: warmup then measure windows; consistent caching/batching policy; pinned versions.
- Regions: NA + EU + one APAC, pending capacity confirmation.

[24:12] Ben Carter: Did I miss anything?

[24:14] Claire Dubois: Add: clear caches between runs (or at least avoid cross-run cache contamination) and document.

[24:20] Rina Kobayashi: Yep.

[24:22] Sean Gallagher: Add: stop conditions if production metrics degrade.

[24:26] Neha Kapoor: Yes.

[24:29] Ben Carter: Great.

[24:31] Ben Carter: Next steps and owners. Claire to draft workload spec by Friday. Rina to validate harness config list and gaps. Sana to propose variance and rerun thresholds. Sean and Vanessa to draft capacity plan and reserve windows. Elliot/Wei to start doc skeleton and FAQ. Ethan to draft report outline and chart list. Tyler to draft UTM plan.

[25:05] Camila Reyes: Also, let’s identify the reviewers for “claims guidelines.” We’ll probably need Michael from legal, but I’ll handle that offline.

[25:15] Ben Carter: Yep.

[25:17] Elliot Price: Can we get a single source of truth doc for scope? Models/regions/workloads? Otherwise it will drift.

[25:24] Ben Carter: I’ll create a scope page and keep it updated.

[25:29] Wei Chen: And can we decide where the methodology appendix lives? Docs site vs PDF vs both.

[25:35] Camila Reyes: Both. PDF will have a summary; docs will have the full detail.

[25:41] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[25:44] Ben Carter: Okay, we have 30 minutes left. I’ll open it up for questions / concerns.

[25:50] Sana Farid: One concern: time. If we do 3 repeats for everything, plus reruns, plus 2 concurrency settings, it might balloon.

[26:01] Claire Dubois: We can limit sensitivity runs to a subset of models. Like top 3 models by demand.

[26:08] Ben Carter: That’s a good idea.

[26:10] Camila Reyes: Yes. Main report covers full matrix; appendix includes a subset deeper dive.

[26:17] Sean Gallagher: Good for capacity.

[26:20] Jonas Weber: Another concern: token distribution. If we publish “median 300 input tokens,” that’s fine. But we should also show range.

[26:29] Claire Dubois: We can publish percentiles.

[26:33] Elliot Price: That can be a small chart: input/output token distribution.

[26:38] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[26:41] Neha Kapoor: On guardrails: we should decide if benchmark runs are allowed to use burst capacity or must be pinned to dedicated pools.

[26:51] Sean Gallagher: Ideally pinned. If it uses burst, it can affect other workloads.

[26:56] Vanessa Ortiz: Pinned is doable but we need early reservations.

[27:01] Ben Carter: Let’s assume pinned capacity.

[27:04] Camila Reyes: Agree.

[27:06] Rina Kobayashi: For pinned, I need to know which cluster endpoints per region. I can work with SRE.

[27:13] Sean Gallagher: Yep.

[27:16] Wei Chen: Question: Are we including Dedicated/Private in the report? Like, can customers run this in their VPC.

[27:23] Camila Reyes: The report is about Redwood’s hosted regions. But we should mention the same runtime powers Dedicated and Private. We can have a CTA: “Talk to us for dedicated/private.”

[27:35] Jonas Weber: Make sure we don’t imply we benchmarked their private cluster.

[27:39] Ethan Wallace: Right.

[27:41] Ben Carter: Another question: can we include “reliability” metrics, like error rate.

[27:47] Sean Gallagher: If we do, it’s a can of worms. But we can include “success rate during run” as a sanity metric.

[27:56] Claire Dubois: The harness logs error counts. We can report “request success %” in the internal QA, and maybe a note “no significant errors observed.”

[28:06] Sana Farid: That’s fine.

[28:08] Camila Reyes: Ok.

[28:10] Ben Carter: I think we’re good. Unless there’s anything else, we can end early.

[28:16] Elliot Price: One more: chart specs. We need consistent units and colors across web and PDF.

[28:22] Camila Reyes: Design team will handle, but yes: define units. Especially “latency/$.”

[28:29] Ethan Wallace: I’ll include unit decisions in the outline.

[28:33] Ben Carter: Perfect.

[28:35] Ben Carter: Thanks everyone. I’ll send notes with action items. Next sync: Friday scope lock with model/region matrix.

[28:44] Camila Reyes: Thanks.

[28:45] Jonas Weber: Thanks.
